blocks.text: A mountain hydropower station drops water 250 m through a steel penstock and fires it as a thin jet at a wheel less than three metres across; a lowland river barrage with a head of only 6 m passes the same power through a propeller as wide as a house. Different head and flow demand completely different machines. Choosing and sizing them rests on a few relations that you can apply with a calculator.

blocks.markdown: A hydraulic turbine converts the potential energy of water, expressed as the **net head** $H$ (m) across the machine, into shaft power. The available hydraulic power is $\rho g Q H$ for volume flow $Q$ and water density $\rho$. The **overall efficiency** $\eta_o$ accounts for hydraulic, volumetric and mechanical losses. The three main types are the Pelton (impulse), Francis (reaction, radial/mixed) and Kaplan (reaction, axial).

blocks.title: Pelton wheel
blocks.text: A **Pelton wheel** is an impulse turbine: the full net head is converted to kinetic energy in a nozzle, giving a free jet of speed $c_1=C_v\sqrt{2gH}$ ($C_v\approx0.97$ to $0.99$, typical). The jet strikes double-cup buckets on the rim of a wheel at pressure equal to the atmosphere, so there is no pressure change across the runner. The buckets turn the relative flow through nearly $180^\circ$.

blocks.caption: Pelton force and power: U is bucket speed, k the ratio of relative exit to inlet speed (friction), phi the angle by which the exit relative velocity falls short of exactly reversing

blocks.title: Power of a Pelton wheel
blocks.prompt: A jet of water of speed 80 m/s and flow 0.12 m$^3$/s strikes buckets moving at 36 m/s. The buckets reverse the relative flow except for an angle $\phi=15^\circ$ short of full reversal, with no friction ($k=1$). Take $\rho=1000$ kg/m$^3$. Find the power developed.

steps.text: Relative speed of the jet entering the bucket.
Force on the bucket from the momentum change of the relative flow.
Power is force times bucket speed.
Compare with the jet kinetic power.

blocks.answer: The wheel develops about 373.7 kW, which is about 97.3% of the jet kinetic power.

blocks.caption: Hydraulic turbine selection; ranges are typical and overlap, with N_s = N sqrt(P)/H^1.25, P in kW, N in rpm, H in m

blocks.markdown: **Specific speed and selection.** The power specific speed $N_s=N\sqrt{P}/H^{5/4}$ (with $N$ in rpm, $P$ in kW, $H$ in m) is a shape number that is the same for geometrically similar runners at their best efficiency. A small $N_s$ means high head and low flow, a large $N_s$ low head and high flow. For a Pelton wheel, $N_s$ is raised by adding jets, which increases flow at the same head and wheel speed.

blocks.caption: Output shaft power from hydraulic power and overall efficiency, and the dimensional specific speed (typical form)

blocks.title: Hydropower and turbine selection
blocks.prompt: A site has a net head of 250 m and a flow of 2.4 m$^3$/s. The turbine and generator set has overall efficiency 0.88 and runs at 375 rpm. Estimate the power and choose a turbine type.
blocks.answer: The power is about 5180 kW (5.18 MW) and $N_s\approx27.1$. Together with the high head, this indicates a Pelton wheel.

items: Compute the hydraulic power $\rho g Q H$ and apply the overall efficiency to obtain the shaft power.
Compute $N_s$ (or use the head and flow directly) and compare with the typical ranges.
High head and low flow suggest Pelton; medium head Francis; low head and high flow Kaplan.
Check cavitation limits for reaction turbines, which sit below the tailwater level and rely on suction at the draft tube.

blocks.title: Optimum bucket speed
blocks.text: For a Pelton wheel with $k=1$ and a given $\phi$, the power $P=\rho Q(c_1-U)(1+k\cos\phi)U$ is greatest when $U=c_1/2$, because $(c_1-U)U$ is a maximum there. In practice friction and windage move the best efficiency point to about 0.45 times the jet speed (typical). If $U$ reached the jet speed the relative flow would vanish and no force would result.

points: Pelton wheel: jet speed $c_1=C_v\sqrt{2gH}$; force $\rho Q(c_1-U)(1+k\cos\phi)$; power $=FU$, best near $U=c_1/2$.
Specific speed guides selection: low for Pelton (high head, low flow), medium for Francis, high for Kaplan (low head, high flow).

questions.stem: For an ideal Pelton wheel with a frictionless bucket that fully reverses the relative flow, at what bucket speed is the power from a jet of speed $c_1$ a maximum?

options.text: At a quarter of the jet speed, $U=c_1/4$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the product (c1 minus U) times U is greatest at half the jet speed.
distractorRationale.b: The relative velocity would be zero, so no force and no power result.
distractorRationale.c: The buckets would move away faster than the jet and no force could be exerted.
distractorRationale.d: The product $(c_1-U)U$ is not a maximum there; the maximum is at $c_1/2$.

questions.explanation: With full reversal and no friction, $P=2\rho Q(c_1-U)U$, which is maximised at $U=c_1/2$. At that speed the outgoing water leaves with zero absolute velocity, so all the jet's kinetic energy has been transferred.

questions.stem: A run-of-river site has a net head of only 8 m and a large flow. Which turbine type is most appropriate?

options.text: Pelton, an impulse turbine with a single jet
Pelton, with the flow shared by six jets
Francis with a small runner, chosen because it is the most compact

distractorRationale.a: A Pelton wheel needs a high head and a small flow.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it is the high specific speed axial machine for low head.
distractorRationale.c: Multiple jets raise the flow capability, but a Pelton wheel still needs high head to be efficient.
distractorRationale.d: The Francis range is for medium head; at 8 m with a large flow the specific speed is too high.

questions.explanation: Low head and high flow give a high specific speed, which is the domain of axial-flow Kaplan or propeller turbines with adjustable blades. A Pelton wheel is an impulse machine suited to heads of hundreds of metres.

questions.stem: A hydroelectric station has a net head of 60 m and a flow of 10 m$^3$/s through one unit of overall efficiency 0.90. Taking $\rho=1000$ kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, the shaft power is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Omits the overall efficiency, giving the hydraulic power.
distractorRationale.b: Divides by $g$ a second time, which is not part of the power formula.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: hydraulic power multiplied by the overall efficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Is off by a factor of ten from a decimal slip.

questions.explanation: Hydraulic power is $\rho gQH=1000\times9.81\times10\times60=5.886$ MW. The overall efficiency of 0.90 reduces this to 5.297 MW.

questions.stem: A turbine runs at 750 rpm, produces 3000 kW at a net head of 100 m. Using $N_s=N\sqrt{P}/H^{5/4}$ and the typical ranges in the lesson, the specific speed is about 130 and the best type is:

distractorRationale.a: Pelton specific speeds are typically below about 60.
distractorRationale.b: Kaplan specific speeds are typically above about 300.
distractorRationale.c: Not a high-speed turbine suited to this head and power.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the value of about 130 lies in the Francis range.

questions.explanation: $H^{5/4}=100^{1.25}=316.2$ and $\sqrt{3000}=54.77$, so $N_s=750\times54.77/316.2=130$. This lies in the medium range, which indicates a Francis turbine.

questions.stem: If the bucket speed of a Pelton wheel were increased until it equalled the jet speed, the force and power on the wheel would:

options.text: fall to zero, because the jet would no longer have any velocity relative to the buckets
be at their maximum, because the bucket speed equals the jet speed
double, because the buckets absorb the full jet speed
be unchanged, because the flow rate is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: fall to zero, because the jet would no longer have any velocity relative to the buckets

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with no relative velocity there is no momentum change and no force.
distractorRationale.b: The maximum is at about half the jet speed, since the force $\propto(c_1-U)$ vanishes at $U=c_1$.
distractorRationale.c: The force depends on the relative speed, not the absolute jet speed.
distractorRationale.d: The momentum change per unit mass depends on $c_1-U$, which would be zero.

questions.explanation: The force is $\rho Q(c_1-U)(1+k\cos\phi)$ and vanishes at $U=c_1$. Power, the product of force and bucket speed, is therefore also zero; the maximum lies between zero and $c_1$.

questions.stem: A Pelton turbine has a net head of 420 m and a nozzle velocity coefficient $C_v=0.97$. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the jet speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: The ideal jet speed is $\sqrt{2gH}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times420}=90.78$ m/s. The coefficient reduces it to $0.97\times90.78=88.05$ m/s.

questions.stem: A jet of water ($\rho=1000$ kg/m$^3$) of speed 85 m/s and flow 0.10 m$^3$/s strikes Pelton buckets moving at 38 m/s. Friction reduces the relative speed leaving the bucket to 0.95 of the inlet value ($k=0.95$) and the bucket turns the relative flow so that the exit is $15^\circ$ short of full reversal. Find the power developed in kW.
questions.explanation: Relative inlet speed is $85-38=47$ m/s. The force is $1000\times0.10\times47\times(1+0.95\cos15^\circ)=9012.9$ N, and the power is $FU=9012.9\times38=342.5$ kW.

questions.stem: A small hydro scheme must deliver 12.0 MW of shaft power at a net head of 180 m with an overall efficiency of 0.90. Taking $\rho=1000$ kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the required flow in m$^3$/s.

A utility has three sites: (A) a net head of 400 m with a small stream, (B) 80 m with a moderate river and (C) 5 m with a very large flow. Using specific speed, explain which turbine type suits each site and why. Describe how the shape of the runner changes as specific speed increases.
markingGuide: Defines specific speed N_s = N sqrt(P)/H^(5/4) as a shape number; large for high flow and low head
Site A: high head, low flow, low N_s, Pelton impulse turbine with one or a few jets
Site B: medium head and flow, medium N_s, Francis reaction turbine
Site C: low head, high flow, high N_s, Kaplan or propeller turbine with axial flow and adjustable blades
Runner shape: from narrow buckets on a large wheel to a radial-inflow runner to a wide axial propeller as N_s increases
Notes typical ranges as approximate and overlapping, and mentions cavitation or efficiency over the load range
questions.explanation: Specific speed grows with flow and falls with head. Site A is high head and low flow (low $N_s$, Pelton), site B in between (Francis) and site C low head and high flow (high $N_s$, Kaplan). The runner passes from a small number of jets striking buckets to a radial runner to a wide axial propeller as the passage area per unit head increases.

questions.stem: For a Pelton wheel with relative-flow reversal factor $(1+k\cos\phi)$ constant, show that the power is a maximum at $U=c_1/2$ and find the maximum power in terms of $\rho$, $Q$ and $c_1$ when $k=1$ and $\phi=0$. Explain why real wheels run slightly below $c_1/2$.
markingGuide: P = rho Q (c1 - U)(1 + k cos phi) U
Differentiates with respect to U: dP/dU proportional to c1 - 2U, zero at U = c1/2 (second derivative negative so maximum)
With k = 1 and phi = 0, P_max = rho Q (c1/2)(2)(c1/2) = rho Q c1^2 / 2
This equals the jet kinetic power so the ideal efficiency is 100 percent
At U = c1/2 the exit absolute velocity is zero in the ideal case
Real wheels run at about 0.45 c1 because friction (k < 1), windage and a jet that does not strike all the buckets at ideal angles change the optimum and the exit velocity
questions.explanation: The product $(c_1-U)U$ has its maximum at $U=c_1/2$, giving $P_{max}=\tfrac12\rho Qc_1^2$ for an ideal wheel, equal to the jet kinetic power. With friction and a bucket angle short of $180^\circ$, the optimum shifts slightly lower and the efficiency is below 100 per cent.
